newsitem.title: USA: U.S. puts Elk Hills oil field stake up for sale.
newsitem.headline: U.S. puts Elk Hills oil field stake up for sale.

text.p: The Energy Department Wednesday began the auction of its stake in California's giant Elk Hills oil field, saying it wanted offers by Oct. 1.
The sale is expected to be one of the largest U.S. government divestures since the privatisation of Conrail, which was sold for $1.6 billion 10 years ago.
"My personal expectation is that this will be the largest privatisation in the history of the United States," Assistant Energy Secretary Patricia Fry Godley said at a news briefing.

The Elk Hills Naval Petroleum Reserve near Bakersfield, Calif., produces almost 60,000 barrels per day of oil and more than 350 million cubic feet per day of natural gas and is one of the largest fields in the lower 48 states.
Godley said she expected competition for the government's interest to be robust as the department's investment bankers had already received more than 200 inquiries about the sale.
"This is a unique property that investors in domestic oil and gas interests in this country want," she said.
The department said it would offer its 78 percent stake in the Elk Hills field in two types of interests. The remaining 22 percent is owned by San Francisco-based Chevron Corp.
Elk Hills was set aside as part of the government's petroleum reserves in the early 1900s to ensure a long-term source of oil for the Navy.

It has been operated commercially for the last 20 years, with the government selling oil and natural gas from the field, an important source of crude oil for California refiners, in a regular bidding process.
Under the sale, the government will offer a single operating working interest that would give the buyer the right to at least 51 percent of each of the field's producing zones.

The rest of its stake would be divided into non-operating working interests, each equivalent to 2 percent of the government's interest in the field. Bidders will be allowed to submit offers on one, some or all of the interests being sold.
The Energy Department said offers would be accepted only on an all-cash basis, payable at closing. All bidders would have to prove they had a net worth of at least $10 million.
The department said it would sell the field only if bids exceeded its minimum sales price, which it expects to set this fall after five independent assessors complete evaluations.
The government's financial advisers for the sale are CS First Boston and Petrie Parkman and Co.
Companies interested in bidding will be invited to technical data presentations in Bakersfield on June 9-12 and in Houston, Texas on June 16-19, the department said.
The government expects to close the sale by Feb. 10, 1998 as required under a law signed last year.
